title: The stars, the moon, the sun, again
hook: Ibrahim's search returns in its full setting (6:74–79)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghayb, the unseen. Your line was not a leaf unknown. Did something small go by that only Allah saw? Today, an old friend comes back. Day four hundred.

Three hundred sixty-eight days ago, on day thirty-two, you met a young man looking up at a star, then the moon, then the sun, watching each one set. You heard him say, I love not things that set. That was the scene on its own, like a single photo. Today the Qur'an hands you the whole roll of film. Because in surah six, the star is not where the story begins. It begins with an argument between a son and his father, and it ends with a question about who is truly safe.
screen: `DAY THIRTY-TWO, AGAIN.` → `THE WHOLE ROLL OF FILM.` → `A SON, A FATHER, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Verse seventy-four. Ibrahim says to his father, whom this verse calls Azar: do you take idols as gods? I see you and your people in plain error. Commentators differ on the name Azar: some take it as his father's name, others as a title or another relative, since the Bible calls Abraham's father Terah. Then verse seventy-five: Allah showed Ibrahim the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who are certain. Only then comes the night sky: the star, the moon, the sun, each one setting. And when the sun goes down, Ibrahim turns. In Pickthall's words: “Lo! I have turned my face toward Him Who created the heavens and the earth,” as one upright by nature, and not one of those who set up partners. Muslims know that line well. In many traditions of the prayer, it's part of the opening supplication, said right after the first Allahu akbar. Then his people argue with him, and he asks them a question: which of us has more right to feel safe? Me, who fears no idol, or you, who don't fear associating partners with God? Verse eighty-two answers: those who believe and don't mix their faith with wrongdoing, they have safety. A hadith in Bukhari says that verse frightened the companions: which of us has never done wrong? And the Prophet ﷺ explained that the wrong here means associating partners with God. Verse eighty-three closes the scene: that was Our argument, which We gave Ibrahim against his people. So the stars were never just stargazing. They were Ibrahim's answer, given in the place everyone could see it: the sky.
screen: `IBRAHIM AND AZAR.` · `SHOWN THE KINGDOM OF THE HEAVENS.` · `I HAVE TURNED MY FACE.` · `WHO HAS MORE RIGHT TO SAFETY?` · then, large: `LOVE WHAT DOESN'T SET.`

segments.voice: If you can, watch the sunset tonight. If not, sit now and picture the last one you remember. Go back to day thirty-two in your mind: the star, the moon, the sun. What were you holding onto then that has since set? A worry, a plan, a person, a phone you loved. Notice it. Then turn your face, even just in your mind, toward what made the sky. The bell holds the time.
The stars. Ibrahim's search in its full setting: the argument with Azar, the kingdom of the heavens shown, the turning of the face, and the question of who is safe. Today's word.
Your line: love what doesn't set. When the sun goes down today, notice it, and remember what you've let go since day thirty-two. Day four hundred.

howItsDone: Many Muslims begin their prayer with a supplication that includes 6:79, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth; Ibrahim's search is a favorite passage for teaching children about the oneness of God.

fork.setup: you hear verse 82: those who don't mix faith with wrongdoing have safety. you're a companion, and you're worried. what do you do?
options: ask the Prophet what the verse means.

original.note: Arabic: I love not things that set (6:76).

trapdoor: what you thought: a young man stargazing.
what it means: a scene framed by an argument with his father and his people, ending in the question of who is truly safe.
what a scholar hears: 6:83 calls the scene Allah's argument (hujjah) given to Ibrahim, which many exegetes cite for reading it as a teaching debate, not a private search.
